heroes.contested: Some historians dispute how much of her work was nursing and how much was running a business, and the comparison with Florence Nightingale remains argued over.

heroes.name: Vivien Thomas
heroes.blurb: Paid as a janitor, he talked the surgeon through the first blue baby operation
heroes.anchor_reason: The day of the first blue baby operation at Johns Hopkins, which he talked the surgeon through.
heroes.story: Vivien Thomas grew up in Nashville and learned carpentry from his father. He was saving for college when the Depression wiped out his savings. In 1930 he took a job as a laboratory assistant to a surgeon named Alfred Blalock. He taught himself surgery on animals and soon ran the lab. Johns Hopkins had no job title for a Black surgical researcher, so for years he was listed and paid as a janitor. In the 1940s a doctor named Helen Taussig asked whether surgery could help babies born with a heart defect that turned their skin blue. Thomas worked out the operation on dogs, doing it about two hundred times until it was reliable. On November 29, 1944, Blalock operated on a fifteen month old girl named Eileen Saxon. He had never done the procedure on a person. He insisted that Thomas stand on a step stool behind him and talk him through each step. The child turned from blue to pink on the table. Thomas got no credit in the published paper. Hopkins gave him an honorary doctorate in 1976. He gave up decades of recognition and fair pay so the work itself could go on.

heroes.name: Frank Serpico
heroes.blurb: New York police officer who refused bribes and testified against his own department
heroes.anchor_reason: The day he gave his main public testimony to the Knapp Commission on police corruption.
heroes.story: Frank Serpico joined the New York City police in 1959. He soon found that officers around him took regular payments from gamblers, drug dealers, and shop owners. He refused to take the money. He reported what he saw to his superiors, then to the mayor's office, and nothing changed. In 1970 he went to the New York Times, and the newspaper printed a front page story on the payments. The city set up the Knapp Commission to investigate. In February 1971, during a drug raid, Serpico was shot in the face while his fellow officers stood nearby and did not help him. He survived, deaf in one ear and with bullet fragments in his head. On December 14, 1971, he put on his only suit and testified before the commission for three hours. He said police corruption could not exist unless it was tolerated higher up, and that no honest officer could speak without fear of reprisal. He left the department the next year and lived abroad for a decade. He gave up his career, his safety, and the trust of the men he had served with.
heroes.contested: Whether the officers with him during the 1971 shooting deliberately failed to help him has never been proven either way.

heroes.name: Eugene Lazowski
heroes.blurb: Faked a typhus epidemic to keep the Germans out of a dozen Polish villages
heroes.anchor_reason: The day he died, in Eugene, Oregon, at ninety-three.
heroes.story: Eugene Lazowski was a young Polish doctor in the town of Rozwadów during the German occupation. A friend from medical school, Stanisław Matulewicz, had noticed something about the standard blood test for typhus. If you injected a person with a dead strain of a harmless bacterium, their blood would test positive for typhus without making them sick. The Germans feared typhus and would not send people from an infected area to labour camps or the front. So the two doctors began injecting villagers and sending their blood samples to German laboratories. The results came back positive. The Germans declared the area an epidemic zone and stayed away. Lazowski timed the injections so the case numbers rose in winter and fell in summer, the way a real outbreak would. He kept it up for about three years. Around eight thousand people in a dozen villages were spared. He also passed medicine through a fence to Jews in the ghetto behind his house. After the war he moved to Chicago and became a professor of pediatrics. He told almost no one what he had done. He risked being shot, along with his family, every time he sent a sample.
heroes.contested: The figure of eight thousand people saved is an estimate and cannot be checked against records.

heroes.name: Li Wenliang
heroes.blurb: Wuhan eye doctor who warned colleagues about a new virus and was silenced
heroes.anchor_reason: The evening he posted the warning to his medical school group chat.
heroes.story: Li Wenliang was a thirty-three year old eye doctor at Wuhan Central Hospital. On December 30, 2019, he saw a laboratory report on a patient that pointed to a coronavirus like the one that caused SARS. Seven people from a local seafood market were already isolated in his hospital. That evening he posted the report and a lung scan to a private chat group of his old medical school classmates and told them to protect themselves and their families. He asked them to keep it quiet. Someone passed it on, and by the next day it was all over the Chinese internet. On January 3 the police called him in and made him sign a statement admitting he had spread false rumours and disturbed public order. He went back to work. A week later he treated a patient with glaucoma who turned out to be infected. Li fell ill, and on February 7, 2020, he died of the disease he had warned about. The government later cleared his name and called him a martyr. He gave up his safety with the police and then his life to tell his friends the truth.

heroes.name: Roberto Clemente
heroes.blurb: Baseball star who died flying earthquake relief to Nicaragua himself
heroes.anchor_reason: The night his overloaded cargo plane crashed off Puerto Rico on the way to Nicaragua.
heroes.story: Roberto Clemente was the right fielder for the Pittsburgh Pirates and one of the best players of his time. He grew up poor in Puerto Rico and never forgot it. On September 30, 1972, he got his three thousandth hit, in what turned out to be his last regular season at bat. On December 23 an earthquake flattened Managua, the capital of Nicaragua, and killed thousands. Clemente had been there weeks earlier and knew people in the city. He organised relief flights from Puerto Rico. Then he heard that the supplies were being stolen by soldiers of the Nicaraguan government before they reached anyone. He decided to fly with the next load himself, so nobody would dare take it. The only plane he could get on New Year's Eve was an old DC-7 cargo plane with a poor maintenance record, loaded about two tonnes over its limit. It went down in the sea minutes after takeoff on the night of December 31, 1972. All five people on board died. His body was never found. Baseball put him in the Hall of Fame the next year. He gave his life to make sure food and medicine reached strangers.
